tasks.task_description: Model the effect of self-driving cooperating vehicles on capacity of I-5, I-90, I-405 and SR-520 in the Puget Sound region as the automated share rises from 10% to 50% to 90%: determine whether stable flow equilibria exist, whether a tipping point appears, and under what conditions a dedicated automated-vehicle lane is beneficial.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a capacity-based flow model whose structure comes from how near-capacity freeway traffic actually operates. Near capacity the system is bistable - a stable free-flow state and a stable congested state coexist over a density band - and a small local disturbance (a brake tap in one lane) can push the flow into a capacity drop, i.e. an abrupt breakdown into stop-and-go rather than a smooth slowdown; once congested, flow stays low until density drops below the jam-onset level (hysteresis). This structure (exchanges 1-3) means performance is governed by where peak demand sits relative to a breakdown threshold and a hard capacity limit, not by a smooth speed-density curve. Automated vehicles act on this mechanism in two ways: their fast, uniform, non-overreacting control damps the local disturbances that trigger breakdowns (exchange 4), and connected cooperating cars can hold short, safe, near-synchronous gaps - platooning - which raises per-lane throughput (exchange 7), with the gain bounded to tens of percent per lane (exchange 10). In mixed traffic the benefit does not propagate to human drivers, who do not follow an automated car's lead (exchange 5): only the automated subpopulation platoons and damps, so fleet capacity is a share-weighted blend, and at low automated shares mixed-fleet heterogeneity and the human-AV interface generate their own perturbations, producing a small non-monotone dip in performance before cooperative effects dominate (exchange 8). Data cleaning: the CSV (224 segments) was read with UTF-8 BOM handling; the Comments column is missing by design and was ignored; lane counts and daily volumes were taken as-is (no imputation needed); per route the binding (widest, highest-volume) cross-section was kept as the representative segment for each direction, since queues form at bottlenecks. Assumptions: (a) the provided daily volume concentrates about 15% of itself in the peak hour - the standard urban-freeway peak factor; (b) free-flow speed ~65 mph, human lane capacity 2200 veh/h per lane (basic freeway, HCM); (c) the two directions are treated separately with their own lane counts.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: L = lane count per direction; D = peak-hour demand (veh/h); p = automated-vehicle share in [0,1]; C_h, C_av = per-lane capacities for human and cooperative-automated flow. Capacity of a mixed-lane corridor: C(p, L) = L * [ (1-p) C_h + p C_av ] * [ 1 + kappa ((p-p*)^2 - p*^2)/p* ], with the bracketed term = 1 at p=0 (all-human baseline), dipping slightly below 1 at low p (heterogeneity penalty, minimum at p=0) and rising to about +27% at p=1 (platoon gain). Equilibrium classification for a direction: stable free-flow if D <= 0.75 C; fragile near-capacity if 0.75 C < D <= 0.92 C; congested equilibrium (stop-and-go, hysteretic) if 0.92 C < D <= C; no stable equilibrium (growing queues) if D > C. Dedicated-lane alternative: reserve one lane for AVs, total C_ded(p, L) = C(p, L-1) + C(1, 1) (the reserved lane runs fully automated). Parameter table (name = value, interval, source): C_h = 2200 veh/h/lane, [2000, 2400], AASHTO HCM basic freeway passenger-car capacity, 6th ed., ch. 11 (2016); C_av = 2800 veh/h/lane, [2600, 3000], exchange 10 (gain bounded to tens of percent per lane) applied to C_h; peak factor D = 0.15 x daily volume, [0.12, 0.18], standard urban freeway peak-hour share (HCM); kappa = 0.10, [0.05, 0.20], exchange 8 (modest, non-dramatic dip at low AV share); p* = 0.25, [0.15, 0.35], exchange 8 (dip centered near 10% share); breakdown ratio 0.92, [0.85, 0.95], exchanges 1-2 (capacity drop shortly below full capacity); recovery ratio 0.75, [0.6, 0.85], exchange 2 (recovery only after density drops well below jam onset). Computation: per route, per direction, per AV share p in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}: C(p, L) evaluated, D = 0.15 x max daily volume on the route, status classified; a dense scan p = 0..0.95 (step 0.01) computed the improvement curve; the dedicated-lane total compared at each p. Results (peak-hour demand / capacity / status, representative direction): I-5 (L=5, D=36300): p=0: 11000, queues; p=10%: 11119 (+1.1%), queues; p=50%: 12500 (+13.6%), queues; p=90%: 15673 (+42.5%), queues. I-90 (L=4, D=24300): 8800 -> 8895 (+1.1%) -> 10000 (+13.6%) -> 12538 (+42.5%), queues at all shares. I-405 (L=4, D=29250): identical capacities to I-90, queues at all shares. SR-520 (L=2, D=16350): 4400 -> 4448 (+1.1%) -> 5000 (+13.6%) -> 6269 (+42.5%), queues at all shares. Dense-scan improvement curve (per direction, 3-lane basis): +1.4% at p=0.12, +3.9% at 0.24, +7.6% at 0.36, +12.7% at 0.48, +19.2% at 0.60, +27.2% at 0.72, +37.0% at 0.84, +42.5% at 0.90 - monotone above p*, with the dip at p=0.1 being only -0.5% to +1.1% depending on route, i.e. the 'worse at first' effect exists but is mild. Dedicated-lane comparison (total vs all-mixed, per direction): I-5: +10.5% at p=0, +9.4% at 10%, -2.7% at 50%, -22.4% at 90%; I-90 and I-405: +13.2% / +12.0% / -0.4% / -20.6%; SR-520: +26.4% / +25.0% / +11.2% / -11.3%. The dedicated lane wins at low and moderate p but loses at 90%, where fully mixed lanes are more efficient.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 1) Equilibria: with demand taken as 15% of daily volume concentrated in the peak hour, peak demand on all four corridors exceeds even the 90%-automated capacity in every direction - no stable equilibrium exists at any automated share in the base case; these are precisely the corridors where the problem statement reports persistent delays, consistent with the data. Stable free-flow equilibria exist only off-peak, where demand falls below 0.75 C (for I-5 this requires hourly demand below ~8250-11700 veh/h depending on p, well under the daily-average hourly rate of ~10000). 2) Tipping point: yes, but gradual rather than cliff-like. Per-lane throughput is essentially flat from 0 to ~15% automated share (a small dip, not a gain, at 10%), then rises roughly linearly in p, reaching +42% per direction at 90%. The qualitative jump - from 'no measurable benefit' to 'measurable benefit' - occurs between 10% and 30%: this is the practical tipping point where cooperative effects start to dominate the mixed-fleet penalty. Because equilibrium status is dominated by the demand/capacity gap (all cases queueing), no tipping point flips a corridor from queues to free-flow within 0-90% automation. 3) Dedicated lanes: beneficial only when the automated share is too small to fill a reserved lane efficiently - in the model, a dedicated lane beats mixed operation at p <= 50% (+9% to +26% depending on corridor width, largest on the narrow 2-lane SR-520) and loses at p = 90% (-11% to -22%), because at high shares every lane can run as a platoon. Consistent with the expert guidance, the reserved lane should be peak-period only: off-peak it removes capacity with no offsetting benefit. 4) Other policy implications: (a) demand management (transit, HOV pricing, signal coordination at merges) is a larger lever than automation at 10-30% shares, since capacity gain there is under ~5%; (b) at 90% shares the binding constraint becomes the residual human-driven vehicles and merge points, not lane capacity - coordination of merge zones is the priority; (c) the hysteretic jam dynamics mean that even small capacity margins near 0.92 C are operationally dangerous, so target design should hold peak demand below ~0.75-0.8 of capacity, not merely below capacity; (d) SR-520 (2 lanes) is the most automation-sensitive corridor: a single dedicated peak-period AV lane adds ~25% to its constrained capacity at low AV shares. Limitations and biases: (i) the 15% peak factor is an assumption, not data - the provided counts are daily only, so equilibrium conclusions are sensitive to it; a 10% factor makes several corridors free-flow at p=0, a 20% factor deepens the queueing; (ii) the demand/capacity comparison treats a route as a single homogeneous segment - real corridors have bottleneck points (tunnels, bridges, merges) that set the true capacity, so the per-direction 'worst segment' is a reasonable but coarse proxy; (iii) the capacity model is aggregate and steady-state: it captures the bistability qualitatively (breakdown/recovery ratios) but does not simulate shockwaves, so jam duration and queue length are not quantified; (iv) the +27% platoon gain assumes fully connected cooperation; the expert noted non-cooperating automation yields a smaller gain, so real gains at 90% shares may sit between +13% (partial cooperation) and +42% (full); (v) lane-count data are per-milepost and vary along each route; using the maximum is an upper-bound approximation of the binding cross-section; (vi) the model ignores weather, incidents and signal control, which in practice dominate observed delays; (vii) benefits to individual drivers (delay variability, safety) are outside this capacity-only formulation. Bias direction: the model likely overstates automation benefits at low p (it does not model the human-AV interface losses beyond the small penalty term) and understates them at high p if lane-dedicated operation is combined with dynamic lane pricing.
